lessons.title: Domino Theory: Eisenhower and Kennedy in Vietnam

before.exam_tip_html: For a 12-mark Source Utility question on Eisenhower or Kennedy in Vietnam, examiners want all three of content, provenance and your own contextual knowledge. Avoid the trap of just labelling a source ‘biased’ — weigh what the source actually says (content), who produced it and why (provenance), and what you know that supports or qualifies it (context). A US State Department briefing and a Buddhist eyewitness account are useful in different ways for different questions; explain what each is good for, not just what each is bad for.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source A.

Source A: An extract from a press conference given by President Dwight D. Eisenhower, Washington DC, 7 April 1954, taken from the Public Papers of the Presidents.
‘You have a row of dominoes set up. You knock over the first one, and what will happen to the last one is the certainty that it will go over very quickly. So you could have a beginning of a disintegration that would have the most profound influences. The loss of Indochina, of Burma, of Thailand — this would lead to the loss of the whole region.’

Using Source A, identify two reasons Eisenhower gives for treating Indochina as vital to American interests.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two clearly distinct reasons drawn precisely from the source, supported by short embedded references.
Secure: Two relevant reasons identified from the source with brief support.
Developing: One clear reason; second point vague or repeats the first.
Emerging: General comment about the source without identifying specific reasons.

Indicative content:
• Loss of one country in the region would trigger the rapid fall of others (the ‘row of dominoes’ image).
• The ‘disintegration’ would have profound regional influences beyond Indochina itself.
• Specific neighbouring countries — Burma, Thailand — were named as next at risk.
• The danger applied to ‘the whole region’, framing Indochina as a strategic test case.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source B.

Source B: An extract from a memorandum by Robert McNamara, US Secretary of Defense, to President Kennedy, dated November 1961, drawn from the Foreign Relations of the United States series.
‘The loss of South Vietnam to communism would not only destroy SEATO but would undermine the credibility of American commitments elsewhere. The struggle there is hard, but it is winnable through advisers, training and the resettlement of the rural population away from Vietcong influence.’

Source C: An extract from an interview given by Buddhist monk Thich Tri Quang to a Western journalist in Hue, July 1963, published in a French magazine.
‘Diem treats Buddhists as foreigners in our own country. His Catholic family rules; his soldiers fired on our people in May. Strategic Hamlets are prisons. We do not want communism, but neither will we accept this.’

Evaluate the usefulness of Sources B and C to a historian studying US involvement in South Vietnam under Kennedy. Use the sources and your knowledge of the period in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained evaluation of both sources weighing content, provenance and contextual knowledge; reaches a substantiated judgement on the usefulness of each.
Secure: Clear evaluation of both sources using all three elements (content, provenance, knowledge); judgement made.
Developing: Some evaluation but tends to handle two of the three elements; judgement may be implicit.
Emerging: Describes the sources or comments on bias only; little integration of own knowledge.

Indicative content:
Source B — Content: McNamara frames Vietnam as a test of US credibility and presents adviser policy as winnable. Provenance: a private memo from Defense Secretary to President, intended to shape policy not public opinion — useful for showing how Domino-Theory thinking dominated decisions. Own knowledge: adviser numbers rose from around 800 to over 16,000 between 1960 and late 1963; Strategic Hamlets launched 1962.
Source C — Content: shows the religious and political grievances that Strategic Hamlets and Diem’s rule provoked. Provenance: a Buddhist monk to a French journalist, July 1963 — first-hand and contemporary, but partial to the protest movement. Own knowledge: the May 1963 Hue shootings, Thich Quang Duc’s self-immolation in June, and Madame Nhu’s ‘barbecues’ remark all confirm the picture.
Judgement: B is highly useful for elite policy thinking but optimistic; C is highly useful for showing the political reality on the ground that Washington was missing.

practice_questions.text: Construct a chronological explanation of how the United States moved from supporting France in Indochina in 1954 to backing the overthrow of Diem in November 1963.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analytical narrative linking three or more events as a chain of cause and consequence; precise factual detail (Geneva, MAAG, Strategic Hamlets, Buddhist crisis); arrives at the November 1963 coup through a substantiated sequence.
Secure: Three or more linked events with causal connectives and accurate detail.
Developing: Events listed in roughly the right order; causal links partial.
Emerging: Thin or muddled chronology with little linking.

Indicative content:
• 1954: Geneva split Vietnam at the 17th parallel; the US replaced France as the South’s patron.
• 1955: Diem became president of South Vietnam with US backing and refused 1956 elections.
• Late 1950s: MAAG advisers trained the ARVN; aid flowed in.
• 1960: Vietcong (NLF) formed in the South.
• 1961–1963: Kennedy raised advisers from c.800 to over 16,000.
• 1962: Strategic Hamlets launched; alienated the rural population.
• May–June 1963: Hue shootings and Thich Quang Duc’s self-immolation discredited Diem internationally.
• 1–2 November 1963: South Vietnamese generals overthrew Diem with US tacit consent.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source D.

Source D: An extract from a National Security Council briefing prepared for President Kennedy in early 1962, drawn from declassified CIA records.
‘The Strategic Hamlet Programme, modelled on British success in Malaya, will physically separate the peasantry from the Vietcong. Within eighteen months we expect a substantial reduction in insurgent recruitment and food supply across the Mekong Delta.’

Source E: An extract from a US adviser’s field report to the Pentagon, October 1963, drawn from the Pentagon Papers.
‘The hamlets in this province are already failing. Many were built so quickly they cannot be defended. Officials have stolen the funds. Peasants resent being uprooted from ancestral land. The VC walk in and out as they please.’

Write an essay on the question: ‘The failure of the Strategic Hamlets programme was the main reason US policy in Vietnam was in crisis by November 1963.’ Using Sources D and E and your own knowledge, evaluate the claim.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained argument addressing the specific claim; integrates content, provenance and own knowledge from both sources; reaches a substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: Clear argument with relevant use of both sources; judgement reached and supported.
Developing: Some argument with reference to both sources but use of provenance or own knowledge limited.
Emerging: Describes sources or events without engaging with the specific claim.

Indicative content:
Supporting the claim:
• Source D shows the optimistic forecast for the Strategic Hamlets programme; Source E shows that within eighteen months it had collapsed in practice.
• Hamlets alienated peasants, were corrupted by officials and were infiltrated by the VC — turning a counter-insurgency tool into a recruitment tool for the other side.
Challenging the claim:
• Diem’s wider political failures were equally or more decisive: refusing 1956 elections, persecuting Buddhists, concentrating power in his family.
• The May–June 1963 Buddhist crisis (Hue shootings, Thich Quang Duc) destroyed Diem’s international reputation independent of the hamlets.
• Structural issue of Domino-Theory thinking meant that any local failure became a strategic crisis.
Judgement: hamlets were a major symptom but the deeper crisis was political — Diem’s regime could not generate legitimacy with or without the hamlets.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source F.

Source F: An extract from a cable sent by US Ambassador to South Vietnam Henry Cabot Lodge to Washington, late August 1963, drawn from the Foreign Relations of the United States series.
‘We are launched on a course from which there is no respectable turning back: the overthrow of the Diem government. There is no possibility of any further effective collaboration with him. Our task is to manage the transition so that the war effort is not weakened.’

Identify two ways in which Source F is useful to a historian studying the end of the Diem regime.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two clearly developed points using content and provenance, reinforced by precise own knowledge.
Secure: Two clear points; uses content and either provenance or own knowledge; some development.
Developing: Two points but undeveloped, or one point fully and one weakly.
Emerging: One general point or surface description.

Indicative content:
• Content: shows that by August 1963 the senior US official on the ground had concluded Diem must go — useful evidence that the US tacitly authorised the coup.
• Provenance: a private cable from Ambassador to Washington, two months before the coup, written for policy not for the public — likely to capture genuine intent.
• Own knowledge: the generals struck on 1–2 November 1963 and Diem was murdered in an armoured personnel carrier; this matches Lodge’s expectation of a managed transition.
• Limitation: a single ambassador’s view; broader Washington debate about whether to encourage or restrain a coup is hidden behind this confident summary.

practice_questions.text: Construct a chronological explanation of how the Buddhist crisis of 1963 transformed US attitudes towards Diem between May and November of that year.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analytical narrative with three or more linked events showing causation; precise dates and details (Hue, Thich Quang Duc, Madame Nhu, Lodge cable, the November coup).
Secure: Three or more linked events; some causal connectives; mostly accurate.
Developing: Events listed in rough order; causal links partial.
Emerging: Thin chronology, weak linkage.

Indicative content:
• 8 May 1963: South Vietnamese troops fired on Buddhists marking the Buddha’s birthday in Hue, killing several.
• 11 June 1963: monk Thich Quang Duc self-immolated in Saigon; the photograph appeared worldwide.
• Summer 1963: Madame Nhu publicly mocked the protests as ‘barbecues’, deepening the international outrage.
• August 1963: US Ambassador Lodge cabled that there could be ‘no further effective collaboration’ with Diem.
• Autumn 1963: Washington signalled it would not stand in the way of a coup.
• 1–2 November 1963: South Vietnamese generals seized power; Diem and Nhu were assassinated.
• 22 November 1963: Kennedy was assassinated in Dallas, leaving the Vietnam decision to Johnson.

lessons.title: Johnson's War: Tonkin and Rolling Thunder

before.exam_tip_html: For an 8-mark Narrative Account, examiner reports flag ‘and then... and then...’ chronologies as the typical mid-band ceiling. To reach the top band, link three or four developments with explicit causal connectives — ‘this triggered’, ‘as a result’, ‘which made it more likely that’. For Tonkin to Rolling Thunder, you need at least: the Tonkin incident, the resolution, the Pleiku attack, the launch of Rolling Thunder, the Da Nang landing — with a causal sentence between each step.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source A.

Source A: An extract from a televised address by President Lyndon B. Johnson to the American people, 4 August 1964, drawn from the Public Papers of the Presidents.
‘Repeated acts of violence against the armed forces of the United States must be met not only with alert defence, but with positive reply. That reply is being given as I speak to you tonight. We seek no wider war.’

Using Source A, identify two reasons Johnson gives for ordering retaliation against North Vietnam.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two distinct reasons drawn precisely from the source, supported by short embedded references.
Secure: Two relevant reasons identified with brief support.
Developing: One clear reason; second vague or repeats the first.
Emerging: General comment about the source.

Indicative content:
• ‘Repeated acts of violence’ against US armed forces required a response.
• Defensive measures alone were not enough — a ‘positive reply’ was needed.
• Retaliation was already underway as he spoke.
• Johnson framed the action as limited (‘we seek no wider war’) to reassure the public.

practice_questions.text: Construct a chronological explanation of how the Gulf of Tonkin incident in August 1964 led to the launch of Operation Rolling Thunder in March 1965.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analytical narrative linking three or more events as a chain of cause and consequence; precise factual detail (Maddox, Tonkin Resolution, Pleiku, Rolling Thunder, Da Nang); arrives at the bombing campaign through a substantiated sequence.
Secure: Three or more linked events with causal connectives and accurate detail.
Developing: Events listed in roughly the right order; causal links partial.
Emerging: Thin or muddled chronology.

Indicative content:
• 2 August 1964: USS Maddox engaged North Vietnamese torpedo boats in the Gulf of Tonkin.
• 4 August 1964: a second alleged attack — later judged to have been false sonar — was reported.
• 7 August 1964: Congress passed the Gulf of Tonkin Resolution 88-2, authorising ‘all necessary measures’.
• Late 1964: instability in Saigon and Vietcong gains increased pressure for escalation.
• 7 February 1965: Vietcong attack on the US base at Pleiku killed several Americans.
• 2 March 1965: Operation Rolling Thunder began as the bombing response.
• 8 March 1965: 3,500 US marines landed at Da Nang to protect the airbase — the first official ground combat troops.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source B.

Source B: An extract from a memorandum by Robert McNamara, US Secretary of Defense, to President Johnson, dated November 1965, drawn from the Pentagon Papers.
‘The bombing has not significantly damaged Hanoi’s capacity to support the war in the South. Infiltration on the Ho Chi Minh Trail has if anything increased. We must consider whether continuation of Rolling Thunder serves our political objectives.’

Source C: An extract from an interview with a North Vietnamese road-repair brigade leader, given to a sympathetic French journalist in 1967 and later published in Hanoi.
‘The bombs come; we hide. The bombs go; we rebuild. A bridge takes one night to mend. Half a million of our women work the roads. The Americans cannot stop us by air alone — they would need to invade, and they will not.’

Evaluate the usefulness of Sources B and C to a historian studying the impact of Operation Rolling Thunder. Use the sources and your knowledge of the period in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained evaluation of both sources weighing content, provenance and contextual knowledge; reaches a substantiated judgement on the usefulness of each.
Secure: Clear evaluation of both sources using all three elements; judgement made.
Developing: Some evaluation but tends to handle two of the three elements.
Emerging: Describes the sources or comments on bias only.

Indicative content:
Source B — Content: McNamara concedes Rolling Thunder has not damaged Hanoi’s war effort. Provenance: a private memo from Defense Secretary to President in 1965, intended for policy not public — useful for showing internal doubt at the highest level. Own knowledge: 864,000 tonnes of bombs dropped 1965–68; the Pentagon’s own analysts later judged it a strategic failure.
Source C — Content: shows the North’s capacity to absorb bombing through dispersal and rapid repair. Provenance: a brigade leader interviewed by a sympathetic French journalist for Hanoi publication — partial but with first-hand experience. Own knowledge: an estimated 500,000 mainly women worked road repair; the Ho Chi Minh Trail was never cut by air power alone.
Judgement: B is highly useful for elite policy doubt; C is highly useful for ground-level explanation of why bombing did not work, but its propaganda framing must be acknowledged.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source D.

Source D: An extract from a press dispatch by an American war correspondent embedded with US marines, sent from Da Nang in summer 1965 and published in a major US newspaper.
‘Our boys patrol jungle in temperatures over 100 degrees, drinking from canteens, listening for trip-wires. The enemy is everywhere and nowhere. We bomb suspected positions and find empty bunkers. The peasants smile by day and disappear at night.’

Source E: An extract from a National Security Council briefing for President Johnson, January 1968, drawn from declassified records.
‘Westmoreland reports an enemy ‘crossover point’ is approaching — the moment when our kill rate exceeds North Vietnamese ability to replace losses. Body counts in IV Corps support this projection.’

Write an essay on the question: ‘The main reason US ground forces could not defeat the Vietcong was the failure of the search-and-destroy strategy.’ Using Sources D and E and your own knowledge, evaluate the claim.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained argument addressing the specific claim; integrates content, provenance and own knowledge from both sources; reaches a substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: Clear argument with relevant use of both sources; judgement reached and supported.
Developing: Some argument with reference to both sources but use of provenance or own knowledge limited.
Emerging: Describes sources or events without engaging with the specific claim.

Indicative content:
Supporting the claim:
• Source D shows the operational reality — a guerrilla enemy that could not be fixed in place; bombing struck empty bunkers.
• Vietcong tactics (tunnels, trails, night movement, peasant integration) negated US firepower.
• Body-count metrics encouraged inflated kill claims that misled commanders.
Challenging the claim:
• Source E shows that senior commanders genuinely believed the strategy was working into 1968 — the failure was as much intelligence as strategy.
• Air power constraints (no bombing of Haiphong/Hanoi until 1972) limited the wider campaign.
• Strategic Hamlets and political instability in Saigon meant the South had no legitimate government to defend.
• Soviet and Chinese aid replaced North Vietnamese losses faster than the US could inflict them.
Judgement: search-and-destroy was a major cause but the deeper failure was the strategic mismatch between conventional firepower and a political-guerrilla war.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source F.

Source F: An extract from a 1965 BBC television documentary on the Ho Chi Minh Trail, presented by a British journalist who had travelled along it.
‘The trail is not a road. It is a thousand paths through forest and mountain, by truck, by bicycle, by porter. American bombs crater it; men with shovels fill in the craters. Each month the trail carries more rifles, more rice, more men south than the month before.’

Identify two ways in which Source F is useful to a historian studying why US bombing failed to cut Vietcong supply lines.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two clearly developed points using content and provenance, reinforced by precise own knowledge.
Secure: Two clear points; uses content and either provenance or own knowledge; some development.
Developing: Two points but undeveloped, or one point fully and one weakly.
Emerging: One general point or surface description.

Indicative content:
• Content: shows the trail was not a single target but a dispersed network — useful evidence for why bombing could not cut it.
• Content: shows monthly tonnage of supplies was rising despite US air strikes.
• Provenance: BBC documentary by a journalist who travelled the trail — first-hand observation, although British public broadcasting may have its own perspective.
• Own knowledge: the trail ran through Laos and Cambodia, beyond Westmoreland’s legal authority to invade; Nixon’s 1969–70 secret bombing of Cambodia was a later attempt to fix exactly this problem.

practice_questions.text: Construct a chronological explanation of how US ground troop numbers in Vietnam grew from 16,000 advisers under Kennedy to over 500,000 combat troops under Johnson.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analytical narrative with three or more linked events showing causation; precise dates and figures.
Secure: Three or more linked events; causal connectives; accurate.
Developing: Events listed in rough order; causal links partial.
Emerging: Thin chronology.

Indicative content:
• Late 1963: Kennedy left around 16,000 US advisers in South Vietnam.
• August 1964: Tonkin Resolution gave Johnson legal authority for force.
• February–March 1965: Pleiku attack triggered Rolling Thunder.
• 8 March 1965: First combat troops — 3,500 marines — landed at Da Nang.
• End of 1965: 184,000 US troops in country.
• End of 1966: 385,000 troops.
• 1967: over 485,000 troops; Westmoreland’s attrition strategy at full scale.
• 1968: peak of 540,000 troops — despite which the Vietcong launched the Tet Offensive that January.

lessons.title: Search and Destroy, My Lai and Protest

before.exam_tip_html: For the 16-mark Source-Based Essay, examiner reports are clear: source-only or knowledge-only answers cap at mid-band. The top band requires you to weave both. Use one source to establish a point of view, then bring in your own knowledge to support, qualify or counter it — before doing the same with the second source. Always reach a substantiated overall judgement on the specific claim in the question, not just on whether the war was good or bad in general.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source A.

Source A: An extract from a New Yorker magazine article by journalist Seymour Hersh, published 20 November 1969, drawn from his investigation into the events at My Lai.
‘On 16 March 1968 Charlie Company entered a Vietnamese hamlet known as My Lai 4. They found no enemy. They killed, by their own subsequent admissions, hundreds of civilians: women, children, the very old. The army called it a battle. The army called the dead enemy. It was a massacre.’

Using Source A, identify two ways in which Hersh challenges the army’s official account of My Lai.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two clearly distinct ways drawn precisely from the source, supported by short embedded references.
Secure: Two relevant points identified with brief support.
Developing: One clear point; second vague.
Emerging: General comment about the source.

Indicative content:
• Hersh notes that there was no enemy present (‘no enemy’) — contradicting the army’s claim of a battle.
• Hersh names the dead as civilians — women, children, the elderly — rather than enemy combatants.
• Hersh draws on the soldiers’ own admissions as evidence.
• Hersh directly relabels the event as ‘a massacre’, not a battle.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source B.

Source B: An extract from a US Army press release describing the My Lai operation, dated 17 March 1968, drawn from the records of the 23rd Infantry Division.
‘American Division forces engaged a strong enemy unit at My Lai 4 yesterday morning, killing 128 Vietcong in a sharp four-hour action. Light US casualties. The hamlet was a long-suspected Vietcong stronghold.’

Source C: An extract from the testimony of warrant officer Hugh Thompson Jr to a US army inquiry, given in late 1969 and drawn from declassified court-martial records.
‘I saw soldiers shooting civilians who were trying to surrender. I landed my helicopter between them and ordered my crew to fire on our own troops if the killing did not stop. The dead were old men, women and small children. There were no enemy fighters in that hamlet.’

Evaluate the usefulness of Sources B and C to a historian studying the events at My Lai. Use the sources and your knowledge of the period in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained evaluation of both sources weighing content, provenance and contextual knowledge; reaches a substantiated judgement on the usefulness of each.
Secure: Clear evaluation of both sources using all three elements; judgement made.
Developing: Some evaluation but tends to handle two of the three elements.
Emerging: Describes the sources or comments on bias only.

Indicative content:
Source B — Content: claims a four-hour engagement and 128 Vietcong dead. Provenance: an army press release issued the day after the events — primary evidence of how the army initially framed the massacre. Own knowledge: the operation was concealed for over a year; the body-count metric encouraged officers to classify civilians as enemy dead.
Source C — Content: directly contradicts B with eyewitness detail of unarmed civilians and an absence of enemy fighters. Provenance: sworn testimony to an army inquiry by a witness whose helicopter intervention saved lives — high credibility, given under oath. Own knowledge: between 350 and 504 civilians were killed; Hersh broke the cover-up in November 1969; only Calley was convicted.
Judgement: B is highly useful for understanding the cover-up itself; C is highly useful for the events. Read together they show how systematically the army misreported the massacre.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source D.

Source D: An extract from a speech by Martin Luther King Jr at Riverside Church, New York, 4 April 1967, drawn from the King Center archive.
‘The bombs in Vietnam explode at home. They destroy the dream and possibility for a decent America. We are taking the young Black men crippled by our society and sending them eight thousand miles to guarantee liberties they have not found in Georgia.’

Source E: An extract from a Gallup opinion poll report, October 1967, drawn from the Roper Center for Public Opinion Research.
‘For the first time, more Americans (46%) say the United States made a mistake in sending troops to Vietnam than say it did not (44%). Disapproval is highest among college graduates and people under 30, but is rising in every demographic group.’

Write an essay on the question: ‘The My Lai massacre was the main reason American public opinion turned against the Vietnam War.’ Using Sources D and E and your own knowledge, evaluate the claim.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained argument addressing the specific claim; integrates content, provenance and own knowledge from both sources; reaches a substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: Clear argument with relevant use of both sources; judgement reached and supported.
Developing: Some argument with reference to both sources but use of provenance or own knowledge limited.
Emerging: Describes the sources or events without engaging with the claim.

Indicative content:
Challenging the claim:
• Source E shows public opinion had already turned against the war by October 1967 — a year before My Lai and two years before Hersh exposed it.
• Source D shows civil-rights leaders linking Vietnam to racial inequality from 1967 — the moral case predated the massacre.
• Earlier turning points: Tet Offensive January 1968 (contradicted official optimism), Cronkite report February 1968, mounting US dead, the draft’s impact on working-class and Black communities.
Supporting the claim:
• My Lai (revealed November 1969) confirmed the worst suspicions and gave anti-war activists undeniable evidence.
• Haeberle’s photographs reached every front page; opinion polls fell sharply after publication.
• Calley’s prosecution, conviction and Nixon’s intervention deepened the credibility crisis.
Judgement: My Lai accelerated and crystallised opposition that was already strong; Tet, the draft and televised reporting were earlier and arguably deeper causes.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source F.

Source F: An extract from a memoir by a US infantry sergeant who served in Vietnam in 1967, published in 1985.
‘Body count was everything. The captain wanted twenty before he wrote his report. We learned to count anyone we found in a free-fire zone, fighter or farmer. After a while you stopped asking who they were. The numbers went up. The war went on. We knew we were not winning anything that could be measured.’

Identify two ways in which Source F is useful to a historian studying the failures of search-and-destroy.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two clearly developed points using content and provenance, reinforced by precise own knowledge.
Secure: Two clear points; uses content and either provenance or own knowledge; some development.
Developing: Two points but undeveloped.
Emerging: One general point or surface description.

Indicative content:
• Content: shows how the body-count metric distorted reporting — civilians counted as enemy dead.
• Content: shows soldiers themselves doubted the strategy was working.
• Provenance: a soldier’s memoir written in 1985, with hindsight and likely shaped by post-war reflection — useful for veteran perspective but not a contemporary record.
• Own knowledge: Pentagon analysts later concluded that perhaps a third of body-count entries were uninvolved civilians; the Tet Offensive 1968 exposed Westmoreland’s ‘crossover point’ claims as illusory.

before.content_html:
The Calm Before

By the end of 1967 General Westmoreland was telling the American press that the war had reached a ‘crossover point’. Body counts, he insisted, now exceeded the rate at which Hanoi could replace its losses. The Vietcong, in his telling, were broken and the war was being won. President Johnson echoed the message. To restore confidence, Westmoreland was flown back to Washington in November 1967 to brief Congress on the ‘light at the end of the tunnel’. Behind the optimism, North Vietnamese commanders were planning the largest combined operation of the war.

The Offensive Itself

On the night of 30 January 1968, the Vietnamese New Year holiday of Tet, around 84,000 Vietcong and North Vietnamese Army troops simultaneously attacked more than 100 cities, towns and military bases across South Vietnam. The traditional Tet ceasefire was used as cover. Targets included Saigon itself: a Vietcong commando squad blasted its way into the US Embassy compound and held part of the grounds for six hours. Television crews filmed the wreckage at the heart of supposedly secure South Vietnam.

The most prolonged fighting was in the imperial city of Hue, which the North Vietnamese held for 25 days. US marines and ARVN troops retook the city block by block. Civilian casualties were heavy and a mass grave was later discovered containing some 2,800 South Vietnamese officials, teachers and Catholics executed by Vietcong cadres during the occupation. Khe Sanh, a US marine base near the Laotian border, was simultaneously besieged for 77 days; its relief tied down US forces who could otherwise have responded faster to the city attacks.

Key Fact

On the night of 30–31 January 1968, around 84,000 Vietcong and NVA troops attacked more than 100 cities, towns and bases across South Vietnam during the Tet ceasefire. Targets included the US Embassy in Saigon, the imperial city of Hue (held for 25 days) and the besieged marine base at Khe Sanh.

A Tactical US Victory

In purely military terms, Tet was a disaster for the communist side. Within weeks the Vietcong had been driven back from almost every position they had briefly seized. They lost an estimated 40,000–50,000 dead and most of their experienced cadres — the southern guerrilla movement was so badly damaged that for the rest of the war the burden of fighting fell on the regular North Vietnamese Army. The hoped-for popular uprising in the South never materialised. By any measurement of ground retaken or enemy losses, the United States and ARVN had won.

For two months, every American newspaper showed images of an enemy that was supposed to be broken: a Vietcong commando dead inside the US Embassy; the chief of South Vietnam’s national police executing a captured suspect on a Saigon street with a pistol shot to the head, photographed by AP photographer Eddie Adams; flames pouring from the city of Hue. None of this matched what Westmoreland and Johnson had told the public for months. The gap between official claims and televised reality became known as the credibility gap.

Walter Cronkite and the Loss of Public Confidence

Walter Cronkite was the anchor of CBS Evening News and routinely described as the most trusted man in America. He travelled to Vietnam in February 1968 and broadcast a special report on 27 February titled ‘Report from Vietnam: Who, What, When, Where, Why?’ His conclusion was unambiguous: the war was ‘mired in stalemate’ and the only rational course was a negotiated settlement. The Cronkite report is reported to have prompted Johnson to remark privately that if he had lost Cronkite, he had lost middle America.

Westmoreland responded to Tet by requesting 200,000 more troops. Johnson rejected the request and instead announced, in a televised address on 31 March 1968, a partial halt to bombing of North Vietnam, an opening to peace talks — and his decision not to seek re-election. Westmoreland was reassigned in June 1968. The strategic landscape had shifted decisively, even though the Vietcong had been militarily defeated on the ground.

Key Fact

On 27 February 1968 Walter Cronkite told American viewers the war was ‘mired in stalemate’. On 31 March 1968 President Johnson announced a partial bombing halt, peace talks — and his decision not to seek re-election. Tet had been a tactical defeat for the Vietcong but had broken Johnson’s political position.

The 1968 Election and Its Consequences

Johnson’s withdrawal from the race opened the field. Anti-war Senator Robert Kennedy was assassinated in June. The Democratic Convention in Chicago in August dissolved into riots between police and anti-war protesters, broadcast live. Republican Richard Nixon won the November election narrowly, promising ‘peace with honour’. Tet had not won the war for Hanoi militarily, but it had ended the Johnson presidency and brought to the White House a Republican who would campaign on extracting the United States from Vietnam.

Two photographs in particular fixed Tet in American memory. Eddie Adams’s image of General Nguyen Ngoc Loan executing a captured prisoner on a Saigon pavement won the 1969 Pulitzer Prize. Footage of the destruction of Ben Tre — the town reportedly described by an unnamed major with the line ‘it became necessary to destroy the village to save it’ — became a symbol of the absurdity many Americans now saw in the war. Together these images captured what statistics could not: the war America had been told it was winning did not match what the cameras showed.

Study Source A.

Source A: An extract from a televised commentary by CBS Evening News anchor Walter Cronkite, broadcast 27 February 1968, drawn from the CBS News archive.
‘To say that we are mired in stalemate seems the only realistic, if unsatisfactory, conclusion. To say that we are closer to victory today is to believe, in the face of the evidence, the optimists who have been wrong in the past. It is increasingly clear to this reporter that the only rational way out then will be to negotiate.’

Indicative content:
• The war is in ‘stalemate’ rather than being won.
• Past official optimism (‘the optimists’) has been repeatedly wrong.
• Claims that the US is closer to victory contradict the evidence.
• A negotiated settlement is the only rational path forward.

Study Source B.

Source B: An extract from a Military Assistance Command Vietnam (MACV) press briefing in Saigon, 1 February 1968, drawn from declassified army records.
‘The enemy attacks of last night will turn out to be his last desperate effort. He has thrown his reserves against well-defended targets. ARVN units have responded vigorously. We expect to see significant Vietcong losses in the coming hours.’

Source C: An extract from a North Vietnamese Army officer’s after-action report on the Tet Offensive, written in March 1968 and released to historians by Hanoi in the 1990s.
‘Our forces in many provinces took heavy losses and could not be replaced. The expected popular uprising did not occur. Yet the political effect in the United States has been greater than we hoped. The Americans no longer believe their own generals.’

Evaluate the usefulness of Sources B and C to a historian studying the impact of the Tet Offensive. Use the sources and your knowledge of the period in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained evaluation of both sources weighing content, provenance and contextual knowledge; reaches a substantiated judgement on the usefulness of each.
Secure: Clear evaluation of both sources using all three elements; judgement made.
Developing: Some evaluation but tends to handle two of the three elements.
Emerging: Describes the sources or comments on bias only.

Indicative content:
Source B — Content: predicts a desperate enemy effort and significant Vietcong losses. Provenance: an MACV briefing on the day of the offensive itself, intended to reassure the press — useful for showing how the US military framed Tet at the moment, but written without knowing the strategic outcome. Own knowledge: 84,000 enemy troops attacked more than 100 targets; the Vietcong did indeed take catastrophic losses (40,000–50,000) but the strategic effect was the opposite of what MACV expected.
Source C — Content: concedes military disaster but identifies the political victory in the US. Provenance: a Hanoi after-action report by an NVA officer, intended for internal use, only released decades later — high credibility because the North had no incentive to be honest about its losses to itself unless honest analysis was needed. Own knowledge: Cronkite’s 27 February report, Johnson’s 31 March withdrawal and Westmoreland’s reassignment all confirm the political effect.
Judgement: B is useful for the immediate American framing but unreliable on outcome; C is highly useful as a candid assessment of why a tactical defeat became a strategic victory.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source D.

Source D: An extract from a press dispatch by an Associated Press correspondent reporting from Saigon, 1 February 1968.
‘Vietcong commandos blasted into the US Embassy compound this morning and held part of the grounds for six hours before being killed. The flag of the United States flew over a battlefield inside the supposedly secure South Vietnamese capital. Millions of Americans watched the footage on the evening news.’

Identify two ways in which Source D is useful to a historian studying why Tet shocked American public opinion.

Secure: Two clear points; uses content and either provenance or own knowledge.

Indicative content:
• Content: shows the Vietcong reached the US Embassy itself — a target presented for years as untouchable.
• Content: shows the events were broadcast on the evening news, reaching millions.
• Provenance: an Associated Press dispatch from Saigon on the day of the attack — first-hand and contemporaneous, written for newspapers across the United States.
• Own knowledge: the Embassy attack was one of more than 100 simultaneous targets; Cronkite’s 27 February report and Johnson’s 31 March withdrawal followed the shift in opinion that televised images like this caused.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source E.

Source E: An extract from President Johnson’s televised address to the nation, 31 March 1968, drawn from the Public Papers of the Presidents.
‘I have ordered our aircraft and our naval vessels to make no attacks on North Vietnam, except in the area north of the demilitarised zone. We are reducing — substantially reducing — the present level of hostilities. I shall not seek, and I will not accept, the nomination of my party for another term as your President.’

Source F: An extract from an interview with a US infantry sergeant who fought in the Hue battle, given in summer 1968.
‘We took the city back, room by room. We knew we had won. Then we got home and the country was telling us we had lost. We could not understand that.’

Write an essay on the question: ‘The Tet Offensive was the turning point of the Vietnam War.’ Using Sources E and F and your own knowledge, evaluate the claim.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained argument addressing the specific claim; integrates content, provenance and own knowledge from both sources; reaches a substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: Clear argument with relevant use of both sources; judgement reached and supported.
Developing: Some argument with reference to both sources but use of provenance or own knowledge limited.
Emerging: Describes sources or events without engaging with the claim.

Indicative content:
Supporting the claim:
• Source E shows Johnson conceding bombing reduction, peace talks and his own withdrawal — a structural shift in US policy directly caused by Tet.
• Westmoreland was reassigned in June 1968; Cronkite’s February report had broken the credibility consensus.
• The Democratic Party split led to Nixon’s November 1968 election on a withdrawal platform.
Challenging the claim:
• Source F shows soldiers’ perception that the battle had been won — militarily Tet was a defeat for Hanoi.
• Earlier turning points: 1965 escalation under Johnson, the rise of the anti-war movement from 1965 onwards, declining poll support since at least 1967.
• Later turning points: My Lai exposure 1969, Cambodia incursion 1970, Paris Accords 1973, fall of Saigon 1975.
Judgement: Tet was decisive politically rather than militarily; it ended the Johnson era and made eventual US withdrawal the only viable policy — even if it took seven more years to complete.

before.content_html:
Nixon’s Promise of ‘Peace with Honour’

Richard Nixon was inaugurated in January 1969. He had won the previous November on a pledge to extract the United States from Vietnam without an obvious defeat. The country was exhausted: over 30,000 US dead, deep public distrust after Tet and Cronkite, and a draft system pulling 19-year-olds into a war their parents no longer believed could be won. Nixon’s strategy had three parts: train and equip the South Vietnamese army to do its own fighting; widen the war into Cambodia and Laos to disrupt enemy sanctuaries; and open diplomatic channels with Hanoi’s Soviet and Chinese backers.

Vietnamisation

Vietnamisation, announced by Nixon in a speech of November 1969, meant phased withdrawal of US ground troops and a major build-up of the ARVN. Between 1969 and 1972 American troop numbers fell from 540,000 to under 50,000. The ARVN expanded to over a million men and was supplied with US helicopters, tanks and air-power coordination. The political logic was simple: bring American boys home while keeping the war going, and the anti-war movement would lose its central grievance.

Key Fact

Vietnamisation was Nixon’s policy of phased withdrawal: from a peak of 540,000 US troops in 1968 to under 50,000 by mid-1972. The ARVN was massively expanded and equipped to take over the ground war, while US air power continued.

Chemical Warfare

From 1962 to 1971 the United States sprayed roughly 80 million litres of Agent Orange over Vietnam, Laos and Cambodia under Operation Ranch Hand. The aim was to strip jungle cover from suspected Vietcong areas and destroy crops. Five million hectares of forest were defoliated. The dioxin in Agent Orange caused cancers, birth defects and chronic health problems among the Vietnamese population and US veterans alike. Spraying was halted under Nixon in 1971 once the medical evidence became impossible to deny.

Cambodia, Kent State and the Limits of Escalation

From March 1969 Nixon authorised secret B-52 bombing of Cambodia — targeting Vietcong sanctuaries along the border. The campaign, called Operation Menu, was concealed from Congress and the American public. In April 1970 Nixon went further: US ground troops crossed the Cambodian border in the Cambodia incursion, an operation Nixon announced on television on 30 April 1970. Far from quietening protest, the announcement reignited the campus anti-war movement.

On 4 May 1970 Ohio National Guardsmen fired on protesters at Kent State University, killing four unarmed students. Photographs of the dead and of fellow student Mary Ann Vecchio screaming over a body went around the world. A nationwide student strike followed; over four million students at 900 campuses walked out. Ten days later, on 14–15 May 1970, two more students were killed by police at Jackson State College in Mississippi — an event widely under-covered by comparison. The Cambodian incursion had transformed domestic politics overnight.

In spring 1972 North Vietnam launched the Easter Offensive, a conventional invasion of the South. Nixon responded with Linebacker II, the so-called ‘Christmas bombings’ of December 1972. For 11 days B-52s pounded Hanoi and the port of Haiphong — the heaviest bombing of the entire war. The aim was to push Hanoi back to the negotiating table, and within weeks the Paris talks resumed. By that point the bombing had also confirmed for many Americans the futility of continued escalation.

The Opening to China

Nixon’s most important diplomatic move had nothing to do with Vietnam directly. In July 1971 his National Security Adviser Henry Kissinger flew secretly to Beijing. The following February Nixon himself made a state visit and met Mao Zedong — the first ever US presidential visit to communist China. The opening exploited the deepening Sino-Soviet split; by improving relations with Beijing, Nixon hoped to pressure both Moscow and Hanoi simultaneously. North Vietnam, dependent on Chinese aid, suddenly had reason to fear that its main backer might prefer better relations with the United States.

Vietnam was the first ‘living-room war’ and Nixon was acutely aware of the medium. Kent State, the Pentagon Papers leaked in 1971 and the conviction of Lieutenant Calley over My Lai all played out on prime-time news. Then in June 1972, five men working for Nixon’s re-election committee were arrested breaking into the Democratic National Committee headquarters in the Watergate building. The slow unravelling of the cover-up over 1973–74 destroyed Nixon’s authority. By the time Hanoi’s next push came in 1975, the United States had no political capacity to act.

Key Fact

Nixon announced the Cambodian incursion on 30 April 1970. Four days later, on 4 May 1970, the Ohio National Guard shot four students dead at Kent State University. A nationwide student strike followed: over four million students at around 900 campuses walked out. Two further students were killed at Jackson State on 14–15 May.

Study Source A.

‘The defence of freedom is everybody’s business — not just America’s business. Under our new policy, we shall provide assistance to those Asian nations capable of and willing to participate in their own defence. The South Vietnamese have continued to gain in strength. Study Source B.

Source B: An extract from a 1972 New York Times news analysis of Nixon’s February 1972 visit to Beijing.
‘The visit changes the shape of the Cold War. Hanoi can no longer assume Chinese support is unconditional. Moscow now competes for American friendship rather than for it. The Vietnam War, while continuing, is no longer the central event of American foreign policy.’

Source C: An extract from a Vietnamese diplomat’s memoir, published in Hanoi in the 1990s, recalling Politburo discussions in spring 1972.
‘Comrade Mao’s reception of the American president disturbed us. We were told the Chinese would maintain their aid — but we were also told to prepare for the possibility that Beijing’s priorities had shifted. We knew the war must now be ended on terms we could secure quickly.’

Evaluate the usefulness of Sources B and C to a historian studying the impact of Nixon’s opening to China on the Vietnam War. Use the sources and your knowledge of the period in your answer.

Mastering: Sustained evaluation of both sources weighing content, provenance and contextual knowledge; reaches a substantiated judgement on the usefulness of each.
Secure: Clear evaluation of both sources using all three elements; judgement made.
Developing: Some evaluation but tends to handle two of the three elements.
Emerging: Describes the sources or comments on bias only.

Indicative content:
Source B — Content: argues the Beijing visit reshaped Cold War alignments and pressured Hanoi. Provenance: a New York Times news analysis written immediately after the visit, for a US public audience — useful for showing how the move was understood at the time, but reflects American framing. Own knowledge: Kissinger had visited Beijing secretly in July 1971; the Sino-Soviet split made the opening possible; Linebacker II in December 1972 followed within ten months.
Source C — Content: shows Hanoi acknowledging the disturbance the visit caused. Provenance: a Politburo-level memoir published in the 1990s, written with hindsight and likely smoothed for publication — useful as the Vietnamese view, but not contemporary documentary evidence. Own knowledge: the Paris Peace Accords were signed January 1973; Hanoi did indeed feel the urgency of a settlement.
Judgement: B is highly useful for immediate US understanding; C is highly useful for the Vietnamese response, with the caveat that hindsight may shape its emphasis. Together they show the opening worked diplomatically even as the war continued.

Indicative content:
• Content: shows National Guardsmen firing on unarmed students within days of Nixon’s Cambodia announcement — useful evidence linking foreign policy decision to domestic violence.
• Content: notes the university closed indefinitely — useful for showing the institutional disruption.
• Provenance: an NBC television report on the day of the shootings — immediate and contemporary, reaching millions of viewers; subject to network editorial choices.
• Own knowledge: over four million students went on strike at around 900 campuses; two further students were shot at Jackson State on 14–15 May; Congress repealed the Gulf of Tonkin Resolution in June.

‘The President is convinced Cambodia was the right call. He is angry at the press coverage but more angry at what he calls the ‘sniveling’ on the campuses. He wants the country to see he is acting decisively. He believes most Americans will support him.’

Source F: An extract from a CBS opinion poll, May 1970, drawn from the Roper Center.
‘58 per cent of Americans disapprove of the Cambodian operation. Only 35 per cent support it. Disapproval has grown ten points since the announcement.’

Write an essay on the question: ‘The decision to invade Cambodia was the most damaging moment of Nixon’s Vietnam policy.’ Using Sources E and F and your own knowledge, evaluate the claim.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained argument addressing the specific claim; integrates content, provenance and own knowledge from both sources; reaches a substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: Clear argument with relevant use of both sources; judgement reached and supported.
Developing: Some argument with reference to both sources but use of provenance or own knowledge limited.
Emerging: Describes sources or events without engaging with the claim.

Indicative content:
Supporting the claim:
• Source F shows public disapproval ran at 58% — clear short-term political damage.
• Source E shows Nixon misread the country, expecting support.
• Cambodia caused Kent State, the four-million-student strike, the repeal of the Tonkin Resolution and the Cooper-Church Amendment — all serious blows to executive war power.
Challenging the claim:
• Watergate (1972–74) was arguably more damaging because it destroyed the political capacity to enforce the 1973 Accords — allowing Saigon to fall in 1975.
• The Christmas Bombings of December 1972 produced comparable international outrage.
• Vietnamisation itself (which preceded Cambodia) had already conceded the strategic war.
Judgement: Cambodia was the most damaging moment for the home front; Watergate was the more damaging for the war’s outcome. The two together undermined Nixon’s entire strategy.

lessons.title: Paris, Saigon and the Price of Conflict

before.content_html:
The Road to Paris

Formal peace talks had opened in Paris in May 1968 after Johnson’s partial bombing halt, but they spent four years deadlocked over procedural questions including the shape of the table. Real movement only came once Nixon’s Secretary of State Henry Kissinger and North Vietnamese negotiator Le Duc Tho began secret bilateral talks in 1970. By the autumn of 1972 a draft agreement was close. Hanoi’s Easter Offensive earlier that year had been beaten back and the Linebacker bombings had increased pressure to settle. South Vietnam’s President Thieu objected fiercely to terms that left North Vietnamese troops inside the South.

The December 1972 Christmas bombings — Linebacker II — were partly aimed at Hanoi and partly at Saigon: showing Hanoi the cost of breaking talks, and showing Thieu that Nixon would still use force on the South’s behalf. By January 1973 the deal was done.

The Paris Peace Accords, January 1973

The Paris Peace Accords were signed on 27 January 1973 by the United States, North Vietnam, South Vietnam and the Vietcong. The terms required: a ceasefire in place; US withdrawal of all military forces within sixty days; return of US prisoners of war; a vague commitment to political settlement between North and South. Critically, North Vietnamese troops already inside the South were not required to leave. Le Duc Tho and Kissinger were jointly awarded the 1973 Nobel Peace Prize; Le Duc Tho refused to accept his.

Key Fact

The Paris Peace Accords, signed 27 January 1973 by the US, North Vietnam, South Vietnam and the Vietcong, required US military withdrawal within sixty days and a ceasefire in place. Crucially, the deal did not require the roughly 150,000 North Vietnamese troops inside South Vietnam to withdraw — effectively conceding the future of the South.

US Withdrawal and the Collapse of Political Will

By 29 March 1973 the last US combat troops had left Vietnam. Around 591 American POWs were returned in Operation Homecoming. Nixon and Kissinger had publicly committed to defend South Vietnam if the North broke the ceasefire — including with renewed bombing. That commitment depended on continuing Congressional support and presidential authority. Both collapsed within eighteen months.

Watergate consumed Nixon. In June 1973 Congress passed the Case-Church Amendment banning further military operations in Indochina without congressional approval. In November 1973 Congress passed the War Powers Resolution over Nixon’s veto, limiting presidential war-making power. On 9 August 1974 Nixon resigned to avoid impeachment. By the time North Vietnam launched its final offensive in spring 1975, Gerald Ford had no political authority and no legal power to renew air support. Congress slashed military aid to Saigon from 2.27 billion in 1973 to 700 million in 1975.

Sensing the opening, Hanoi launched the Ho Chi Minh Campaign in March 1975. The ARVN, starved of fuel, ammunition and air support, collapsed faster than even North Vietnamese commanders had expected. The strategic city of Buon Ma Thuot fell on 10 March; Hue fell on 25 March; Da Nang on 30 March. President Thieu’s order for a strategic withdrawal turned into a rout. Within seven weeks the war was over.

The Fall of Saigon, 30 April 1975

By late April 1975 North Vietnamese armoured columns were on the outskirts of Saigon. President Thieu had resigned on 21 April, accusing the Americans of betrayal. On 29 April the United States launched Operation Frequent Wind, the largest helicopter evacuation in history. Over 18 hours, 7,000 Americans and Vietnamese were lifted from rooftops across the city to the US Seventh Fleet offshore. Iconic photographs of evacuees clambering up a ladder to a helicopter on a CIA building roof became the lasting image of American defeat.

On the morning of 30 April 1975, North Vietnamese tank 843 crashed through the gates of the Independence Palace in Saigon. Two hours later, the new South Vietnamese government broadcast its unconditional surrender. The fall of Saigon ended the war that the Domino Theory had said could not be allowed to happen.

Key Fact

Saigon fell on 30 April 1975. Operation Frequent Wind, the day before, lifted around 7,000 Americans and Vietnamese allies from rooftops across the city in 18 hours. North Vietnamese tank 843 crashed through the gates of the Independence Palace; the war the United States had fought for over a decade ended in unconditional surrender.

The Price of Conflict

The human cost was staggering. Around 58,000 Americans had died, with another 153,000 wounded. An estimated 1.1 million North Vietnamese and Vietcong soldiers, 250,000 ARVN soldiers and 2 million Vietnamese civilians had been killed across all parts of the conflict. Roughly 5 million hectares of forest had been defoliated. Cambodia and Laos suffered tens of thousands of additional dead from US bombing and post-war upheaval — the Khmer Rouge took power in Cambodia in 1975 and killed perhaps 1.7 million people in their own country between 1975 and 1979.

Vietnam was reunified in July 1976 as the Socialist Republic of Vietnam. The new government sent perhaps a million former South Vietnamese soldiers and officials to ‘re-education camps’. Around 800,000 people fled by sea between 1975 and 1995, becoming known as boat people; tens of thousands died in the attempt. Economic collapse, exacerbated by a US trade embargo and the loss of southern entrepreneurial life, was severe. Vietnam fought a brief border war with China in 1979 and occupied Cambodia from 1978 to 1989. The country only recovered economically after the Doi Moi market reforms began in 1986.

The American Reckoning

For the United States, the impact was equally lasting. The ‘Vietnam Syndrome’ — reluctance to commit ground forces in foreign wars — shaped foreign policy for two decades. The Veterans’ Memorial in Washington DC, opened in 1982, listed every American name. The credibility of the executive branch never fully recovered: the War Powers Resolution remained law, congressional scrutiny of intelligence increased, and public scepticism about military adventurism shaped responses to every later crisis from Iran to Iraq.
before.exam_tip_html: For the 16-mark Source-Based Essay on the end of the war, examiner reports specifically warn against monocausal answers. The fall of Saigon was not just a North Vietnamese victory; it was a Southern collapse caused by Watergate-era political weakness, Congressional aid cuts, ARVN structural problems and Hanoi’s strategic patience. Use the sources to set up two competing explanations and bring in your own knowledge to weigh them — then reach a substantiated overall judgement.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source A.

Source A: An extract from a televised address by President Richard Nixon, 23 January 1973, drawn from the Public Papers of the Presidents.
‘At 12:30 Paris time today, the agreement on ending the war and restoring peace in Vietnam was initialled by Dr Henry Kissinger on behalf of the United States, and Special Adviser Le Duc Tho on behalf of the Democratic Republic of Vietnam. We have achieved a peace with honour. The South Vietnamese people have the right to determine their own future, without outside interference.’

Using Source A, identify two claims Nixon makes about the Paris Peace Accords.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two clearly distinct claims drawn precisely from the source, supported by short references.
Secure: Two relevant claims identified with brief support.
Developing: One clear claim; second vague.
Emerging: General comment.

Indicative content:
• The agreement represents ‘peace with honour’ for the United States.
• The South Vietnamese now have the right to determine their own future.
• That right is to be exercised ‘without outside interference’.
• The Accords ended the war and restored peace.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source B.

Source B: An extract from a private memorandum by Henry Kissinger to President Nixon, October 1972, drawn from declassified White House records.
‘The North will not withdraw its troops from the South. We cannot get them to. The best we can secure is a decent interval — a period during which a southern government can survive on its own. After that, the political question must work itself out by Vietnamese means.’

Source C: An extract from an interview with President Nguyen Van Thieu of South Vietnam, given to a Western journalist in spring 1975, shortly before his resignation.
‘The Americans signed a treaty that left their enemy’s army on our soil. They promised us in 1973 they would return if Hanoi broke the agreement. They did not return. Saigon will fall because the United States allowed it to fall.’

Evaluate the usefulness of Sources B and C to a historian studying why Saigon fell in 1975. Use the sources and your knowledge of the period in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained evaluation of both sources weighing content, provenance and contextual knowledge; reaches a substantiated judgement on the usefulness of each.
Secure: Clear evaluation of both sources using all three elements; judgement made.
Developing: Some evaluation but tends to handle two of the three elements.
Emerging: Describes the sources or comments on bias only.

Indicative content:
Source B — Content: shows Kissinger admitted privately that the deal would not save the South in the long run, only buy a ‘decent interval’. Provenance: a private memo from Secretary of State to President in October 1972, never intended for public — high credibility for understanding US elite calculation. Own knowledge: the Accords left around 150,000 NVA troops in the South, confirming the structural concession.
Source C — Content: shows Thieu blaming the United States for breaking its 1973 commitments. Provenance: an interview given by the resigning South Vietnamese president to a Western journalist — partial, intended to shape his historical reputation. Own knowledge: Watergate destroyed Nixon’s authority; the Case-Church Amendment of 1973 banned further US military action; military aid was cut from 2.27 billion in 1973 to 700 million in 1975.
Judgement: B is highly useful for elite US calculation; C is highly useful for the South Vietnamese view, with the caveat that it is partly self-justifying. Read together they support an explanation centring on US political collapse rather than purely on North Vietnamese strength.

practice_questions.text: Construct a chronological explanation of the steps from the Paris Peace Accords in January 1973 to the fall of Saigon on 30 April 1975.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analytical narrative linking three or more events as a chain of cause and consequence; precise dates and details (Accords, Case-Church, Nixon resignation, aid cuts, Spring Offensive, Frequent Wind).
Secure: Three or more linked events with causal connectives.
Developing: Events listed in roughly the right order; causal links partial.
Emerging: Thin chronology.

Indicative content:
• 27 January 1973: Paris Peace Accords signed; NVA troops remained in the South.
• 29 March 1973: last US combat troops left; 591 POWs returned in Operation Homecoming.
• June 1973: Case-Church Amendment banned further US military operations in Indochina.
• November 1973: War Powers Resolution passed over Nixon’s veto.
• August 1974: Nixon resigned over Watergate; Ford took office without political authority for renewed bombing.
• 1973–75: US military aid to Saigon cut from 2.27 billion to 700 million.
• March 1975: Hanoi launched the Ho Chi Minh Campaign; Buon Ma Thuot fell 10 March, Hue 25 March, Da Nang 30 March.
• 21 April 1975: Thieu resigned, blaming US betrayal.
• 29–30 April 1975: Operation Frequent Wind evacuated 7,000 people; Saigon fell as NVA tank 843 crashed through the Independence Palace gates.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source D.

Source D: An extract from a CBS Evening News broadcast by Walter Cronkite, 30 April 1975.
‘Saigon fell to communist forces today. The last Americans were lifted from the embassy roof by helicopter as North Vietnamese tanks rolled through the streets. After more than a decade, more than 58,000 American dead and 150 billion dollars, the war that defined a generation has ended in defeat.’

Identify two ways in which Source D is useful to a historian studying the consequences of the fall of Saigon.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two clearly developed points using content and provenance, reinforced by precise own knowledge.
Secure: Two clear points; uses content and either provenance or own knowledge.
Developing: Two points but undeveloped.
Emerging: One general point.

Indicative content:
• Content: gives the headline figures — 58,000 American dead and 150 billion dollars — useful for the human and financial cost.
• Content: explicitly characterises the war as ending ‘in defeat’ — useful evidence of how mainstream US media framed the outcome immediately.
• Provenance: CBS Evening News on the day of the fall — reaching tens of millions; from the same anchor who had called the war a stalemate seven years earlier in 1968.
• Own knowledge: Operation Frequent Wind lifted 7,000 people; Vietnamese casualties were vastly higher than US (roughly three million dead all causes); the ‘Vietnam Syndrome’ shaped US foreign policy for two decades.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source E.

Source E: An extract from a New York Times opinion editorial, 1 May 1975.
‘Saigon has fallen because South Vietnam was a state without legitimacy, propped up by an outside power that ultimately tired of the burden. To say the United States lost is half the truth. The other half is that the South Vietnamese government never really existed as a self-sustaining state.’

Source F: An extract from a memoir by an ARVN colonel published in 1992, recalling the spring of 1975.
‘We had no fuel for our tanks. We had no air cover after Watergate. The Americans had promised us in 1973 they would return if the North broke the ceasefire. The Americans did not return. We fought without bullets, and we lost.’

Write an essay on the question: ‘The fall of Saigon in 1975 was caused more by the collapse of South Vietnam than by the strength of North Vietnam.’ Using Sources E and F and your own knowledge, evaluate the claim.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained argument addressing the specific claim; integrates content, provenance and own knowledge from both sources; reaches a substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: Clear argument with relevant use of both sources; judgement reached and supported.
Developing: Some argument with reference to both sources but use of provenance or own knowledge limited.
Emerging: Describes sources or events without engaging with the claim.

Indicative content:
Supporting the claim:
• Source E argues South Vietnam ‘never really existed as a self-sustaining state’ — the regime had been propped up since 1955.
• Source F shows ARVN’s structural collapse: no fuel, no air cover, no US support.
• Watergate and the Case-Church Amendment removed US power to enforce the Accords; Congress cut military aid from 2.27 billion to 700 million between 1973 and 1975.
• Diem’s assassination 1963, ARVN corruption, Strategic Hamlets failure all undermined Southern legitimacy.
Challenging the claim:
• Hanoi’s 1975 Spring Offensive was a major conventional operation, executed with disciplined planning — the North did win the war, not just receive it.
• Soviet and Chinese aid to North Vietnam continued at high levels after 1973 while US aid to Saigon was being cut.
• The Tet Offensive and earlier Vietcong campaigns had built the political and military groundwork.
Judgement: the fall combined Hanoi’s patience and conventional capacity with a fatal collapse of US-Southern political will. The structural Southern weakness was exposed once the US guarantee was withdrawn — both factors were necessary, neither alone was sufficient.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source G.

Source G: An extract from the Vietnam Veterans Memorial Fund’s dedication ceremony speech in Washington DC, November 1982.
‘On this wall are the names of 58,272 men and women. Each name is a son or daughter, a husband or wife, a brother or sister. We do not say here whether the war was right or wrong. We say only that these Americans went where their country sent them, and they did not come home.’

Using Source G, identify two purposes of the Vietnam Veterans Memorial.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two distinct purposes drawn precisely from the source, supported by short references.
Secure: Two relevant purposes identified with brief support.
Developing: One clear purpose; second vague.
Emerging: General comment.

Indicative content:
• To list every American killed in the war (the names of 58,272 dead).
• To remember each death as personal — a family member, not a statistic.
• To honour service rather than to take a political position on the war (‘we do not say here whether the war was right or wrong’).
• To recognise that those who died had been ‘sent’ by their country.
